newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Sen leader Lott wants MFN extension for China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Sen leader Lott wants MFN extension for China.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Wednesday he supports a one-year extension of Most Favored Nation trade status for China but will not back a permanent extension at this time. Speaking to the National Association of Manufacturers, the Mississippi Republican also said he wanted to "find a way" to pass the so-called fast-track trade agreement procedures this year without the provisions on labor and the environment sought by Democrats.
Lott told the industry leaders he would also favor expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement to include Latin America.

Talks between the Clinton administration and the Republican-controlled Congress on granting fast-track trade negotiation authority broke down in late 1995 after the two sides could not agree on a compromise over the labor and environment issues. The administration wanted the broadest authority possible to negotiate on those issues in trade deals, while Republicans sought to limit that authority.

A growing number of lawmakers, tired of the annual ritual of reviewing China's MFN status, which allows goods to enter the country at the same low tariff as goods from most other countries, have been voicing support for granting permanent MFN this year.
U.S. businesses, citing uncertainties in their commercial dealings with China, have been lobbying for an end to the annual review.

The annual review has provided a stage for human rights groups to voice their concern about China's record. It also provides lawmakers an opportunity to look at Beijing's record on nuclear technology proliferation and at the yawning trade gap between the two countries.

Administration officials are currently negotiating with China on its entry into the World Trade Organization and some analysts have said it would be premature to grant permanent MFN before that process is complete.

The New York Times, quoting senior administration officials,reported on Wednesday that Chinese authorities have indicated to the U.S. negotiating team they are ready to scrap many trade barriers, including laws protecting some of China's state-and military-run industries from foreign competition.

In Beijing Chinese officials dismissed the report as inaccurate. The Times said the offers had so far been made in conversations with Chinese authorities and that administration officials were wary of Beijing's willingness to follow through with some of the changes discussed.
